<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD for the bisq-cli package follows standard AUR packaging practices. All source URLs point to the legitimate upstream repositories on GitHub (`github.com/bisq-network/`). The `SKIP` checksums are appropriate for VCS (git) sources. The `prepare()` function configures a git submodule to use a locally provided source, which is a standard pattern for AUR packages that need to handle git submodules separately. The `build()` function uses the project's own Gradle wrapper (`./gradlew`) to build the application. No suspicious network requests, obfuscated code, dangerous commands (eval, base64, curl|bash), or unexpected file operations are present. The comment containing a `curl | gpg --import` pipeline is an instruction for the user to import a PGP key manually, not executable code in the build process.
</details>
<evidence>

<summary>Standard AUR PKGBUILD with no malicious indicators</summary>
</security_assessment>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a benign shell launcher wrapper. It sets a default Java home, opportunistically detects HiDPI scaling via local desktop environment interfaces such as GNOME Mutter D-Bus, Sway IPC, and Hyprland IPC, then exports a JavaFX scaling option and executes the Bisq desktop binary under `/opt/bisq-desktop/bin/desktop`.

I do not see suspicious network access, downloads, execution of fetched code, credential access, data exfiltration, obfuscation, or system modification. The hardcoded `/opt/bisq-desktop/bin/desktop` target is consistent with a package-installed application launcher.
</details>
